newsitem.title: USA: Papers offer to take by strikers as jobs open up.
newsitem.headline: Papers offer to take by strikers as jobs open up.

text.p: Detroit's two daily papers Wednesday offered jobs to striking newspaper workers as they become available, but the move was quickly shot down by union officials, who vowed to take the papers to court.
The proposal from Detroit Newspapers Inc., which runs the Detroit Free Press and Detroit News, was issued in response to an unconditional return-to-work offer made by six striking unions Friday.

"Effective immediately, we are prepared to offer any job openings as they occur within each bargaining unit to former striking employees," the papers said in a statement. "These employees will be placed on a preferential hiring list, based on seniority."
Free Press Publisher Heath Meriwether said at a news conference the paper currently has about 10 openings. Robert Giles, editor and publisher of the News did not say how many openings his paper has.

But the Metropolitan Council of Newspaper Unions considered the proposal, one of four made by the papers, a rejection of their offer because it does not immediately offer jobs to all of the 2,500 workers who originally walked off the job.

"The unions have made a good-faith effort to stop the pain and suffering in this community, and the employer again has told us and this community to go to hell," council Chairman Al Derey told a news conference.

Derey said the unions would seek a federal court order forcing the papers to take all the striking workers back. If the papers are found to have committed unfair labour practices, they could be held liable for back pay from the time the unconditional offer was made.

Since the bitter strike began 19 months ago, the papers have hired about 1,200 replacement workers, while more than 400 of the original 2,500 have crossed picket lines. The papers said another 600 jobs have been eliminated through efficiencies, and about 180 people were fired for strike-related misconduct.

The papers also proposed Wednesday to set up a training fund for workers whose jobs have been eliminated through productivity improvements; establish a relocation fund for people who want to work at other papers; and not contest future unemployment claims.
The Free Press, owned by Knight-Ridder Inc. and the News, which is owned by Gannett Co. Inc. have independent newsrooms but are run by a joint operating company.
Striking workers included newsroom, distribution, pressroom and mailroom workers. They walked off the job in July 1995 after contract talks broke down.
